1	# Facts for #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run: every open question needing a browser or iPhone is not runnable here, and none of the rest needs an experiment. `git status` is clean.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	### The tree
8	
9	- A leaked pairing code is short-lived: the window closes on the first successful pairing, after 3 wrong codes, or at 5 minutes. `src/core/remote.rs:46-72` (`Paired` clears `pairing`, "single-use").
10	- `RemoteRequest` is built only inside `src/adapters/remote.rs` (definition `:360`); no test in `tests/` constructs it. Adding `cookie`, `origin` and `user_agent` fields touches the adapter alone. Grep: `RemoteRequest\b` over `src tests`.
11	- `RemoteReply { status, body, authenticated }` is built literally at about 15 sites in `src/app.rs` (e.g. `:1664`, `:2365`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and not in `tests/`. A header field on it needs a `Default` or a constructor, or every site changes.
12	- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` live in `adapters/`, not `ports/` or `model.rs`, so CLAUDE.md's additivity rule for the shared contract does not name them. `src/adapters/remote.rs:355-393`.
13	- `last_message` exists on the session record: the hook binary writes it from `last_assistant_message` (`src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs:37`) and `src/core/tests.rs:1717` constructs records with `last_message: None`. It is not on the wire: no match in `control/` or `client/Sources`. Adding it to `SessionView` is a new field there.
14	- The certificate can be reissued over the same key. `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` is already used at `src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`, the SPKI hash is of the key (`:107`), and `make_identity` (`:95-127`) is the only path that makes a new key. A reissue keeps `spki_sha256`.
15	- `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift`, `switchboard-remote/main.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. `addresses` is read as a list at `ConnectionManager.swift:483` and built as a one-element list at `main.swift:120`. A URL parser can fill `addresses` with the one host:port.
16	
17	### Outside the tree
18	
19	- **Apple's TLS server certificate rules.** SHA-2 signature, RSA at least 2048 bits, the server's DNS name in subjectAltName (CommonName not trusted), and for certificates issued after 1 July 2019 an EKU of `serverAuth` and a validity of at most 825 days. Non-compliant connections fail and "websites [may] not load in Safari". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15; Citrix says iOS 14 / macOS 11 also). The page does not mention IP-address SANs, user-added roots, or exemptions. The current certificate has no SAN, a CN only, and a not-after of year 4096 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`), so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or validity rules.
20	- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
21	  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
22	- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.
23	- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265 says so, quoted on https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies. `Secure` cookies are sent only over HTTPS. `localStorage` is per origin including port (MDN, general). This confirms the notes' cross-port claim.
24	- **WebSocket subprotocol (RFC 6455 §4.1, §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455).**
25	  - The client must fail if the 101 names a subprotocol it did not offer.
26	  - The server's reply is one `token`, and an empty value is illegal.
27	  - Offered values are `token`s, so base64url without padding is legal. Base64 `=` is not a token character (a separator).
28	  - Whether the client must fail when the server returns none is not normative: §4.2.2 says the server sends none when it agrees to none, and §1.9 (non-normative) says it must include it.
29	  - Browsers must send `Origin` on the handshake. A server may validate it, and rejects with 403. "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere."
30	  - The tree's `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) echoes no subprotocol.
31	- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current entry**; Back then shows the new URL and bypasses the old one (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState). It says nothing about what the browser recorded before the script ran.
32	  - Query: "MDN history.replaceState".
33	
34	## Unresolved
35	
36	Each line ends with what the plan builds to. The plan never waits on a line here.
37	
38	1. **Does a click-through exception cover `wss://` and `fetch` on current iOS Safari, with this no-SAN certificate on a bare IP?**
39	   - Tried: the queries above, plus "Safari remember certificate exception visit this website how long self-signed iOS per session". The only evidence is old (2010 bug, iOS 7 and 13 era), the code-server doc (v3.7, 2021), and the one iOS 26 beta post. Nothing current and primary exists.
40	   - Favourable: the page may use the events socket directly. Unfavourable, and the plan must do this anyway: the page works with REST polling alone (poll `changed`-equivalent reads on a timer) and treats the socket as an upgrade it may lose, saying "live updates unavailable" rather than failing.
41	   - Reissuing the certificate with a SAN, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity over the same key is cheap and helps in both cases (Apple's page; the code-server doc).
42	2. **Does a SAN with an IP address, rather than a DNS name, satisfy Safari and Chrome?** The Apple page speaks only of DNS names. Queries: as in 1, plus "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address". No primary source found.
43	   - Favourable: put the LAN IP in the SAN. Unfavourable: the page's URL host must be a `.local` name. Either way the plan reissues with the `.local` hostname as a DNS SAN as well.
44	3. **Does Apple's 825-day rule apply to a manually trusted self-signed leaf?** The page lists no exemption and no scope. Build to a validity of 825 days or fewer and say in the dialog that the certificate is renewed (the key, and so the pin, is unchanged). If it does not apply, nothing is lost.
45	4. **Does a click-through certificate give a secure context in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** The spec reads yes by scheme, but I found no browser documentation on certificate-error overrides. The plan uses `crypto.randomUUID` only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a fallback id generator built on `getRandomValues`, and does not rely on `Secure` cookies being stored without a manual test (see item 5).
46	5. **Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and do `Secure` cookies work on an IP host, in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake; Secure cookie IP address host Safari Chrome Firefox". Results were blogs and a Chromium design thread (WebSocket requests carry cookies; `wss` counts as the same scheme as `https`): leads, not evidence. Plan to either transport behind one server-side reader that accepts the bearer header, the cookie and the subprotocol token, and let the first manual run pick the page's transport.
47	6. **Is the code-bearing URL recorded in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs?** No source. The plan assumes yes: the code is single-use and the window is 5 minutes or 3 failures (settled above), so a recorded URL is dead once pairing succeeds. The plan says that in the dialog and keeps the query out of server logs (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, logs path only).
48	7. **Per-site exception lifetime across launches, and loss when the IP changes.** Query: "Safari remember certificate exception ... how long". Only a 2013 blog (iOS 7: exception not removable). Plan: an address change means another warning, and the page and dialog say so. A `.local` name or a reissue never makes it worse.
49	8. **Pool of 4 under a real page load (iOS Safari parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`).** No source for the connection count; it needs a device. Plan: answer static paths on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, serve the page as few files as possible (HTML plus one script and one stylesheet, inlined where possible by the CSP), and give static paths their own bound so a page load cannot starve `/pair`.
50	9. **Bonjour `.local` resolution from iOS Safari.** No query run, so no evidence. Plan: the URL carries the IP from `local_address()` and the `.local` name only if the owner answers item B below.
51	
52	## For the owner
53	
54	A. **On a real iPhone/iPad, after accepting the warning, does the page load, do `fetch` calls work, and does `new WebSocket("wss://…")` connect, with the current certificate and with the reissued one?** Ask with the page as built. Favourable branch: use the socket. Unfavourable: ship polling. The plan builds the polling path regardless.
55	B. **Does `https://<mac-name>.local:<port>/` resolve from the owner's phone?** Favourable: reissue with that DNS SAN and put it in the URL. Unfavourable: the IP stays the URL host. Reissuing with both works either way.
56	C. **Does the owner's phone camera open the URL straight into Safari, and does the tab appear in iCloud tab sync or history before the page script runs?** Either branch: the code is single-use and expires, so the plan holds.
57	D. **Does a cookie, or a subprotocol token, work in Safari with the owner's certificate (items 5, 1)?** Favourable: use the one that works, the cookie preferred for the token never being readable by script. Unfavourable: use the other; the server accepts all three transports regardless.
58

1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.
103	
104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.

139	
140	- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
141	  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
142	  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
143	  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
144	  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
145	  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
146	  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
147	  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
148	  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
149	  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
150	  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
151	  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
152	  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
153	- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
154	  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
155	  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
156	  `:3116-3118`).
157	- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
158	  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
159	  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
160	  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
161	- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
162	  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
163	  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
164	  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.
165	
166	### Pairing UI and the text paths
167	
168	- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
169	  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
170	  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
171	  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
172	  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
173	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
174	  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
175	  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
176	  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
177	  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
178	  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
179	  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
180	  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
181	- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
182	  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
183	  the payload.
184	- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
185	  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
186	  against a test data dir.

188	### Tests that exist and what extends
189	
190	- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
191	  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
192	  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
193	  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
194	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
195	  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
196	  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
197	  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
198	  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).

200	  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
201	  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
202	  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
203	  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
204	  only by hand.
205	- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.
206

209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).

218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in

231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`

# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes

Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.

## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back

- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
  not to any record.
- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
  address that moves would need another reissue.

## What the code does today, piece by piece

### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)

- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`

  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`

  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
  (that is a question below, not checked).

  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`

  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).

  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
  here.

### The router (`src/app.rs`)

- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles

  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the

- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
  Y").
- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
  new static handler must keep that true.

### The session list and the excerpt

- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
  `:3116-3118`).
- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.

### Pairing UI and the text paths

- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
  the payload.
- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
  against a test data dir.

### Tests that exist and what extends

- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
  only by hand.
- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.

## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open

- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
  not at the connection thread.
- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing (above).
- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
  (above).
- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
  browser, and the spec text must say so.
- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
  service on another port of that host would all receive a
  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
  script on the origin can read it.

497:- A set renamed and a pin moved (saved through `SaveViews`), a Claude Code pane reaching its trust question (`PromptSeen`, no save), and a Codex pane passing its quiet interval (`HostListed`, no save, no screen change): each emits `changed` for the right resource within the pass. Ten passes over a running pane with nothing else moving emit nothing, though `quiet_secs` moved on each.
498:- Two reads of a watched file, a transcript and a pane separated by an external edit with no poll between them, del

1	# Switchboard Remote Client Architecture — v1
2	
3	**Status:** Proposed implementation specification, revised against the repository
4	**Targets:** Switchboard Rust host; native visionOS client; reusable iPadOS client core
5	**Primary objective:** Browse and interact with the sessions and working sets of multiple independently running Switchboard instances, with native spatial windows on visionOS.
6	
7	## 0. Revision notes
8	
9	The first draft was written without the codebase. This revision merges its
10	concepts with what exists:
11	
12	- "Cards" are not a resource. A working-set item is a `PinTarget` (a session
13	  record id, or a project id and a path relative to the project root) with a
14	  grid rectangle; the target is the item's identity. The API speaks
15	  **sessions, projects, working sets with pins, and files reachable only
16	  through a pin**. There is no `card_id`.
17	- The control port (`control/`, `switchboard-control`) already carries most of
18	  this API: `SessionView`, `SetView` with `Pin`s, `ProjectView`, `waiting`,
19	  `session.screen`, `session.send`, `session.resume`, `session.trust`, and
20	  `find` / `op.status`. The remote port is a transport over that contract,
21	  not a second one.
22	- The control port's operation id and `operations.log` are the idempotency
23	  mechanism, extended so that a non-replayable command is logged **before**
24	  it runs (today only creations are logged, and only after).
25	- The host has no Tokio and no HTTP stack. The core is single-threaded and
26	  every request is answered on the frame thread; the remote port keeps that
27	  shape, with bounded queues.
28	- The host has no event bus, and its transcript and screen polling follows
29	  the local view. The port adds a watch set of its own, app-level content
30	  caches that version what they read, a per-process revision counter and
31	  "changed" events with refetch, computed by diffing the exported read
32	  models after every pass rather than by watching for a save. Clients
33	  subscribe before they snapshot.
34	- Security is bound by the repo's existing rules (CLAUDE.md "Hard rules",
35	  design.md "Trust boundary"): one redaction policy covers every text that
36	  leaves the port and runs before any cut, host key material lives in the
37	  Keychain, the certificate
38	  is verified out of band before pairing, and agents are never resumed
39	  without a human.
40	- A spike precedes Milestone A, and no milestone ships a LAN-bound
41	  unauthenticated port.
42	
43	The second review round (the outside reviewer's F1–F6, and a trim) changed
44	this:
45	
46	- Collections are answered whole with bounded fields; the membership
47	  snapshot walk is gone. Only the conversation pages.
48	- The watch set is capped globally with least-recently-read eviction; there
49	  is no `watch_refused` and no "not live" client state.
50	- Content work (parsing, file reads, masking, hashing) runs on the
51	  connection thread, never on the frame; the frame hands out the handle and
52	  the policy and records the version. The frame does core state only.
53	- Content versions for files and logs are inode, ctime and size, not mtime
54	  and length (F2). Pairing codes, tokens, attempt counting and key rotation
55	  are specified (F3). The client keeps content in memory only (F5). A client
56	  workspace may span hosts (F6).
57	- Milestone A is five commits, A0 to A4, with a two-host read-only client at
58	  A2 (F1).
59	
60	## 1. Product goals
61	
62	- Keep agent execution, transcript parsing, filesystem access, and session ownership on the host machines.
63	- Support **multiple concurrently connected Switchboard instances** on a single client, not just a selected active host.
64	- Discover local hosts automatically; allow manually configured hosts.
65	- Provide unified working-set and session browsing, with explicit source-machine identity.
66	- Render native text and controls, not streamed desktop pixels.
67	- Preserve the existing presentation concepts: the compact working-set card, the full last-response view, and the complete navigable conversation for Claude Code sessions.
68	- Allow cards to open as independently movable native visionOS windows.
69	- Reuse the transport, models, authentication, and most SwiftUI components on iPadOS.
70	- Keep v1 local-network-first, but do not bake LAN-only assumptions into the API.
71	
72	## 2. Non-goals for v1
73	
74	- Central server, cloud account, cloud relay, or shared database.
75	- Cross-host session migration or execution of commands on a different host from the session's owner.
76	- Programmatic positioning of visionOS windows in 3D space.
77	- Automatic recreation of exact spatial coordinates.
78	- A new transcript parser. The host parses a transcript whole, as the app does today; §4.3 says what that bounds and what it does not.
79	- Editing working sets, projects, environments or definitions from the client.
80	- Answering Dispatch decisions from the client (the obvious v2; see §4.6).
81	- Full supervisor-driven workspace orchestration.
82	
83	## 3. Core architecture
84	
85	```text
86	Mac A: Switchboard + remote port --\
87	                                     \       Bonjour + HTTPS/WSS
88	Mac B: Switchboard + remote port ----> Native Client (visionOS / iPadOS)
89	                                     /       ConnectionManager
90	Mac C: Switchboard + remote port --/        UnifiedStore
91	                                             Window/PresentationStore
92	```
93	
94	Each host is authoritative for its own resources. The client aggregates views without copying ownership of sessions. One client maintains **one connection state machine and one WebSocket per connected host**. A host going offline must not block other hosts.
95	
96	### 3.1 Identity and namespacing
97	
98	- `server_id`: stable, randomly generated UUID persisted in `<data dir>/identity.json` (its own small file beside `views.json`, so it needs no `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump; written through the store's atomic path). Never derive it from hostname, IP, or Bonjour instance name. A second instance pointed at another `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` therefore has its own.
99	- `identity.json` also holds the host's **certificate** (DER, base64) and the certificate's creation time. The certificate is public; its private key is in the Keychain (§5). The two are made together, once, on first listen. If the key is missing when the certificate is present (a Keychain reset, an unsigned build), the host makes a fresh pair, logs that it did, and the paired-devices dialog says every pairing is now invalid.
100	- `server_name`: user-editable display name, kept in `identity.json` beside the id (A1 chose this over a `Settings` field, which would have needed a `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and a migrate step for one string). The listen preference (loopback or the local network, and the port) lives there too: the file is the remote port's own, read before the app's records matter.
101	- Host-side identifiers are the existing ones and are never renamed on the wire: `RecordId` (a session, stable forever), `ProjectId`, `SetId` (a working set, in `views.json`), `SpaceId`. The host id (the tmux session) and the resume handle (the provider's session id) are never exposed as identity; `resume_id` is informational, as on `SessionView`.
102	- All client-facing references are **qualified**: `(server_id, resource_id)`. A `SessionRef` is `{server_id, record_id}`, a `WorkingSetRef` is `{server_id, set_id}`, a `FileRef` is `{server_id, project_id, path}`.
103	- A single client may show items from multiple servers in one collection, but every command is routed to the item's owning server.
104	- `server_id` identifies a logical installation, **not a trusted cryptographic identity**. Trust is the pinned public key established at pairing (§5).
105	
106	### 3.2 Multi-instance behaviors
107	
108	- Maintain a list of **known servers** (paired and manually added), independent of currently discovered servers.
109	- Discovery adds candidates; it does not automatically trust or authorize them.
110	- Client can connect to all enabled known servers concurrently, reconnecting each independently.
111	- Default unified view includes items from all connected servers; filter by one or more servers.
112	- Show a source-machine label on each card, with a clear offline/stale state.
113	- When a host disconnects, keep its last known items visible as **read-only cached snapshots** with a disconnected indicator. Do not imply that actions succeeded.
114	- When a host reconnects, reconcile the host's authoritative state before re-enabling commands.
115	- Preserve the selected server filters and window/item references across client relaunches.
116	- If two endpoints advertise the same `server_id`, treat them as candidate addresses for one logical server; verify the pinned key before switching endpoints. Do not silently merge untrusted installations.
117	
118	## 4. Rust host
119	
120	### 4.1 Implementation
121	
122	- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
123	- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
124	- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
125	  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
126	  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
127	  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
128	  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
129	  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
130	  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
131	  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
132	- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
133	- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
134	- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
135	- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
136	- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
137	- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
138	- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.
139	
140	### 4.2 API conventions
141	
142	- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
143	- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
144	- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
145	- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
146	- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
147	- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
148	  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
149	  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
150	  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
151	  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
152	  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
153	  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
154	- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
155	- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.
156	
157	### 4.3 Endpoints
158	
159	| Method | Endpoint | Wire body | Scope |
160	|---|---|---|---|
161	| GET | `/api/v1/info` | new: `info` | none (identity only, before pairing) |
162	| POST | `/api/v1/pair` | pairing handshake (§5) | none, only inside the pairing window |
163	| GET | `/api/v1/projects` | `projects`; `?scope=all` includes Dispatch's worker records | read |
164	| GET | `/api/v1/spaces` | `spaces` | read |
165	| GET | `/api/v1/spaces/{id}/sets` | `sets` | read |
166	| GET | `/api/v1/sets/{id}` | new: `set` (the `SetView` with pins) | read |
167	| GET | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` | `sessions`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
168	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}` | `session` | read |
169	| GET | `/api/v1/waiting` | `waiting`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
170	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/screen?lines=n` | `session.screen` | read |
171	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/conversation?from=turn\|last&limit=n`, or `?before=turn&limit=n` | new: `session.conversation` | read |
172	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/conversation/{n}` | new: `session.turn` (one turn with its activity uncut) | read |
173	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/last-response` | new: `session.last_response` | read |
174	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/runs` | new: `session.runs` | read |
175	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/runs/{n}/output?lines=n` | new: `session.run_output` | read |
176	| GET | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/files/{path}` | new: `file.read` (pinned files only) | read |
177	| POST | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` | `session.new` (§4.5) | control |
178	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` | `session.send` | control |
179	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/resume` | `session.resume` | control |
180	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/trust` | `session.trust` | control |
181	| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/draft` | `session.draft` | read |
182	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/draft` | `session.draft` | control |
183	| POST | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/dictation` | `session.dictation` | control |
184	| GET | `/api/v1/ops/{op}` | `op.status` | read |
185	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets` | new: the core's `TicketListing` (§4.7) | read |
186	| GET | `/api/v1/dispatch/tickets/{id}` | new: `TicketDetail` | read |

194	Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.
195	
196	**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
197	  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
198	  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
199	  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
200	  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
201	  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
202	  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".

204	New read models, added to the wire crate:
205	
206	- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
207	- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
208	- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
209	- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
210	  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
211	  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
212	  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
213	  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
214	  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
215	  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
216	  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
217	- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

221	### 4.4 WebSocket events
222	
223	Envelope:
224	
225	```json
226	{
227	  "server_id": "uuid",
228	  "epoch": "uuid",
229	  "revision": 1042,
230	  "type": "changed",
231	  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
232	  "at_ms": 1760220000000
233	}
234	```
235	
236	Event types:
237	
238	- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
239	- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
240	- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
241	- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
242	- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
243	- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.
244	
245	**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:
246	
247	1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
248	2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
249	   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
250	   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
251	   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
252	   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
253	   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
254	3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
255	
256	**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.
257	
258	**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.
259	
260	**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:
261	
262	1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
263	2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
264	3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
265	4. enables commands.
266	
267	Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.
